title: Bitcoin sextortion emails: 'I have your password' blackmail waves — the video does not exist
summary: Mass extortion emails and mailed letters claim to have webcam video of you watching porn and demand bitcoin. The 'proof' is a real old password, apparently pulled from breach dumps — or, since 2024, your name, address, and a map photo of your home with a QR code. The video does not exist. Running since July 2018 and still active: do not pay, do not reply, do not scan the QR code.

impact.victims: 51,146 extortion complaints to IC3 in 2018 (all extortion types; 'the majority' tied to the sextortion email campaign) — the $83M figure is 2018 adjusted losses alone; cumulative losses since have never been totaled as a single figure. Waves have recurred every year since.

timeline.event: First mass wave documented: emails open with the recipient's real password ('I'm aware that [password] is your password'), claim a webcam recording made while the target watched porn, and demand bitcoin — typically a few hundred to a few thousand dollars. The passwords trace to old breach dumps, not a live hack.

IC3 issues PSA I-080718-PSA: extortionists increasingly include recipients' personal information (usernames, passwords) in email and postal-mail threats to appear credible, give ~48-hour deadlines, and demand bitcoin for its perceived anonymity.

FTC publishes 'How to avoid a Bitcoin blackmail scam' on the parallel postal variant: letters mailed to men alleging an affair — 'pay me a $8600 confidentiality fee in Bitcoin' — with instructions for buying bitcoin. FTC: report letters to local police and the FBI. (Verified via Wayback capture; the live page blocks automated fetches.)

IC3 2018 Internet Crime Report quantifies the wave: 51,146 extortion complaints — a 242% increase in extortion complaints over 2017 — with adjusted losses over $83 million; 'the majority of extortion complaints received in 2018 were part of a sextortion campaign.'

IC3 PSA I-040723-PSA warns of the second-layer scam: for-profit 'sextortion assistance' companies charging victims thousands (one juvenile victim paid $5,000; another was charged $2,000 and then $3,200 more) for help that law enforcement and nonprofits provide free, in one case discouraging a victim's mother from contacting police.

Personalization escalates: emails (often PDF attachments) now include the recipient's name, home address, and a street-view photo of their house lifted from online mapping services; demands run ~$1,950–$2,000 in bitcoin via embedded QR code, some claiming 'Pegasus' spyware infection.

EFF confirms the home-photo wave is 'merely a new variation on an old scam': the personal data comes from breaches and public records, not from any compromise of the recipient's devices. Advice: do not pay, do not respond.

NJCCIC alert 'New Year, New Round of Sextortion Scams': the email wave circulates again — threats arrive as PDF attachments named after the target, opening with the recipient's phone number and home address, demanding ~$2,000 in bitcoin within 'one day'. NJCCIC: no indication the threats are credible; do not pay; report to the FTC, IC3, and NJCCIC.

affected: Anyone whose email address and an old password appear in circulated breach dumps — the mail merge targets everyone in the dump, not people who were actually hacked
Recipients who still reuse the quoted password anywhere (the one real risk the email reveals)
Recipients of the postal variants: 'confidentiality fee' affair letters (2018–) and letters/PDFs with a photo of the home (2024–)
People who paid: funds moved on-chain are very unlikely to come back; report the address and txid to IC3
notAffected: You, if you received one and did nothing — there is no video; the sender has never had access to your webcam or files
Your devices: receiving the email or letter infects nothing by itself (do not scan the QR code or follow its links)
People whose quoted password is long-retired and used nowhere — the 'evidence' is a decade-old breach record, not fresh access
Your contacts: no case in the cited advisories shows these bulk senders ever releasing a video, because none exists
actions: Do not pay and do not reply. The 'video' is a bluff run as a mail merge over breach dumps and map data — paying marks you as a payer and invites repeat demands.
If the quoted password is one you still use, change it everywhere now and turn on two-factor authentication; check your exposure at haveibeenpwned.com.
Do not scan the QR code, click links, or open attachments beyond viewing. Mark the email as spam. If it arrived as a physical letter, the FTC says to report it to your local police and the FBI.

Report it free at ic3.gov (include the full email with headers, and the bitcoin address/txid if you paid) and at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Reporting costs nothing and no company can 'remove you from the list'.

If you paid: file with IC3 immediately with the transaction details, then ignore anyone who contacts you offering to recover your bitcoin for a fee — that is the recovery scam, the second half of this one.

If the threat involves real intimate images, that is a different and serious crime: if the target is a minor or the images were taken when they were under 18, use NCMEC's free Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org); adults should use the free StopNCII (stopncii.org). Call 1-800-CALL-FBI, and never pay a for-profit 'sextortion assistance' firm — IC3 warns these companies charge exorbitant fees for what law enforcement and nonprofits do at no charge.

claims.claim: In 2018, IC3 received 51,146 extortion-related complaints — a 242% increase in extortion complaints over 2017 — with adjusted losses over $83 million, and the majority were part of the sextortion email campaign.
For-profit 'sextortion assistance' companies charged victims $2,000–$5,000, fabricated perpetrator demands to justify more charges, and discouraged victims from contacting law enforcement.
The passwords quoted in the 2018 email wave were drawn by script from data breaches more than a decade old.
claims.attribution: KrebsOnSecurity analysis of reader-submitted samples; consistent with EFF's later assessment

claims.claim: Home photos in the 2024 wave are lifted from online mapping/street-view services such as Google Maps, matched to addresses from breach and public-records data.
claims.attribution: KrebsOnSecurity and EFF, from message samples; no operator has been charged for this wave in the cited sources

claims.claim: Some 2024-wave messages claim the target was infected with 'Pegasus' spyware.
